## Learning objectives

1. Describe what a large language model does, and what follows from that.
2. Write a prompt that produces usable R code, using context, constraints and
   examples.
3. Recognise the failure modes: fabricated citations, plausible-but-wrong
   code, silent statistical errors.
4. State what you may and may not put into a commercial AI tool under Indian
   data protection law and institutional policy.
5. Disclose AI assistance in line with ICMJE recommendations.

## What the model is doing

A large language model predicts the next token given the preceding ones,
trained on a very large corpus. It is optimised for **plausibility**, not for
truth. Everything useful and everything dangerous about it follows from that
one sentence.

::: {.callout-important}
## The asymmetry that matters
It is very good at things where plausible and correct coincide — syntax,
boilerplate, translation, restructuring text. It is unreliable where they come
apart — a specific citation, a specific p-value, a claim about a specific
paper. Wrong answers are delivered in exactly the same confident register as
right ones. There is no tell.
:::

## Where it genuinely helps

| Task | Why it works |
|---|---|
| "What does this error mean?" | Common errors are well represented in training data |
| Converting SPSS syntax to R | Structural translation; you can verify the output |
| Regex, `ggplot2` theming, `case_when()` boilerplate | Fiddly, well-documented, instantly checkable |
| Commenting and explaining existing code | You have the ground truth in front of you |
| Improving the clarity of your own prose | You remain the author of the content |
| Drafting a data dictionary from column names | Tedious, low-stakes, easily checked |

The pattern: tasks where **you can verify the answer faster than you could
produce it**. That is the whole test.

## Where it fails, with examples

**Fabricated references.** Ask for five papers on flipped classrooms in Indian
medical colleges and you will get five plausible citations — correct-looking
authors, real journals, wrong or non-existent DOIs. Check every reference
against PubMed or the DOI resolver. Every one, every time.

**Code that runs and is wrong.** Ask for a paired t-test and you may receive an
unpaired one. It executes. It produces a p-value. Nothing warns you.

**Statistical advice without your data.** It cannot see whether your residuals
are normal, whether your clusters are independent, or whether your outcome is
zero-inflated. Advice given without that information is generic advice, and
generic advice is how the wrong test gets applied.

**Hallucinated function arguments.** `tbl_summary(pretty = TRUE)` — confident,
sensible-looking, does not exist. Check against the package documentation.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The competence trap
You cannot check code you could not have written. Using AI to work beyond
your understanding produces output you cannot evaluate — which is precisely
the situation in which errors survive into publication. This is why Day 2
comes after Day 1, and not the other way round.
:::

## Prompting that works

A weak prompt:

> make a plot of my data

A strong prompt:

> I have an R data frame `students` with 240 rows. Columns: `teaching_arm`
> (character, "Flipped classroom"/"Traditional lecture"), `gain` (numeric,
> 11 NAs), `college` (character, 3 levels).
>
> Write tidyverse code using the native pipe `|>` to produce a ggplot2
> boxplot of `gain` by `teaching_arm`, faceted by `college`, with jittered
> points, a colour-blind-safe palette, and publication-quality labels.
>
> Use only ggplot2 and dplyr. Explain the missing-value handling in a
> comment. Do not use `%>%`.

Five ingredients:

1. **Context** — the shape and types of the actual data.
2. **Task** — one specific thing.
3. **Constraints** — packages, style, pipe, what to avoid.
4. **Format** — code with comments, or prose, or a table.
5. **Verification** — ask it to state its assumptions so you can check them.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Two habits worth forming
**Paste the error, not a description of it.** The full message, including the
line number, is far more informative than "my code doesn't work".

**Ask for the assumptions.** "What is this code assuming about my data?" often
surfaces the mistake faster than reading the code does.
:::

## What you must not paste

::: {.callout-important}
## Non-negotiable
Never paste into a commercial AI tool:

- Patient-identifiable data of any kind, including dates of birth and
  hospital numbers
- Student-identifiable assessment data — marks attached to names or roll
  numbers
- Unpublished data belonging to collaborators without their explicit consent
- Anything your ethics approval did not anticipate leaving the institution
- Draft manuscripts under embargo or containing others' unpublished results
:::

Assume that anything you type may be retained and may be used for training
unless you have an enterprise agreement that says otherwise. Consumer chat
interfaces and API endpoints have different terms; institutional deployments
different again. Read yours before, not after.

**The safe pattern:** paste the *structure*, never the *data*.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Share this - column names and types, no values
str(students)

# Or a synthetic extract with the same shape
students |> slice_head(n = 3) |> mutate(across(everything(), ~ "..."))
```

## Legal and ethical frame in India

- **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**: health data is personal
  data. Consent, purpose limitation and the obligations of a data fiduciary
  apply. Pasting identifiable records into an overseas service is a transfer,
  and your institution, not the vendor, carries the obligation.
- **ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research**
  (2017) — data sharing must fall within what participants consented to.
- **ICMJE recommendations**: AI cannot be an author. Authors are accountable
  for all content, including anything AI-assisted. Use must be disclosed in
  the methods or acknowledgements.
- **NITI Aayog's National Strategy for AI** and the **IndiaAI Mission** —
  the policy context: sectoral guidance, compute infrastructure, and an
  explicit health priority.

Journals differ in the detail. Check the specific instructions to authors
before you submit; most now have an explicit AI clause.

## How to disclose

A methods sentence that will satisfy most journals:

> Generative AI (ChatGPT, GPT-4o, OpenAI) was used to draft and debug R code
> for data visualisation. All code was reviewed, executed and verified by the
> authors. No AI tool was used to generate data, interpret results, or draft
> the scientific content of this manuscript. The authors take full
> responsibility for the integrity of the work.

Specific tool, specific use, explicit statement of what it was *not* used for,
explicit acceptance of responsibility. Vagueness helps nobody.

## Discussion

::: {.callout-note title="Discussion: 10 minutes, in groups"}
1. Where in *your* workflow would AI assistance save real time this month?
2. Where would you refuse to use it, and why?
3. Your department wants a one-page AI policy for postgraduate dissertations.
   What are its three rules?

Groups report one sentence each.
:::

## Key takeaways

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
- LLMs optimise for plausibility. Useful where plausible and correct coincide;
  dangerous where they do not.
- Use it for tasks you can verify faster than you could do them. That is the
  entire test.
- Verify every citation. Check every function argument. Read every line of
  code you did not write.
- Never paste identifiable data. Share structure, not values.
- Disclose specifically: which tool, which task, which responsibility.
- The skill that makes AI safe is the skill you spent yesterday building.
:::
